claims.text: High-entropy alloys have an intrinsically homogeneous microstructure.
A homogeneous single-phase or near-single-phase microstructure promotes stable oxide or passive-film formation.
Microstructural homogeneity enables rapid, dynamic formation and self-healing of a protective passive oxide film under mechanical disruption.
High configurational entropy supports continuous regeneration of the passive oxide film.
Mechanical wear intermittently ruptures the passive film.
The alloy composition and homogeneous microstructure cause the ruptured protective oxide to reform rapidly.
Rapid passive-film reformation minimizes exposure of the underlying substrate.
A protective oxide film can reduce wear by providing lubrication or surface protection.
Improved passive-film stability can improve corrosion resistance.
Dynamic film healing synergistically reduces both wear and corrosion relative to their independent action.
Combined wear-corrosion degradation will be lower than the sum of degradation measured in isolated wear and isolated corrosion tests.
Suppressing rapid passive-film reformation through composition changes, inhibitors, or environmental conditions will accelerate combined degradation.
The proposed protection should hold in alloys containing oxide-forming elements and possessing microstructural uniformity.
Extreme mechanical loads can prevent passive-film reformation and cause the protective mechanism to fail.
In isolated wear and isolated corrosion tests, passive-film regeneration is not challenged by mechanical film rupture.
Film rupture and reformation kinetics depend on mechanical stress, corrosive aggressiveness, and minor compositional variations.
If suppressing oxide formation does not significantly increase degradation under otherwise identical wear-corrosion cycling, the proposed governing mechanism is falsified.

contradictions.description: The intervention and mechanism state that mechanical wear ruptures the passive film, whereas the baseline says that specimens under isolated wear are not challenged by mechanical film rupture. Isolated wear would still mechanically disrupt a surface film even without corrosion.
